title: Merge Intervals
oneLinerQuestion: Merge all overlapping intervals in an array.
explanation:
Problem Intuition: The Merge Intervals problem asks us to consolidate an array of intervals into a minimum set of non-overlapping intervals covering the exact same ranges. An unsorted list makes overlap detection difficult because intervals that overlap could appear anywhere in the input. By sorting intervals by their start coordinates, all potentially overlapping intervals are grouped adjacently, allowing us to perform the entire merge process sequentially in a single linear pass.

- Step 1: Interval Sorting — We sort the intervals array in ascending order based on each interval's start value: intervals.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]). Sorting guarantees that for any two consecutive intervals, the first interval always begins before or at the exact same moment as the second.

- Step 2: Merged Array Initialization — We initialize an empty array 'merged = []' to store the consolidated intervals, and we immediately push the very first sorted interval (intervals[0]) into it as our initial reference baseline.

- Step 3: Sequential Interval Traversal — We iterate through the remaining intervals starting from index 1 to intervals.length - 1. For each interval 'current', we compare it against the last interval currently placed in our result set: 'lastMerged = merged[merged.length - 1]'.

- Step 4: Overlap Detection & Interval Merging — If current[0] <= lastMerged[1], the current interval begins before or at the instant the previous interval finishes, meaning they overlap. We merge them by extending the end boundary of the last placed interval: lastMerged[1] = Math.max(lastMerged[1], current[1]).

- Step 5: Disjoint Interval Handling — If current[0] > lastMerged[1], there is a clean gap between the two intervals. Since future intervals will start even later due to the initial sort, 'lastMerged' is completely sealed. We push 'current' directly into 'merged' as a new standalone interval.

- Step 6: Result Output — After scanning all intervals, the 'merged' list contains the comprehensive set of mutually exclusive, ordered intervals spanning the full original domain.

- Complexity & Memory Guarantees — Time Complexity: O(N log N) dominated by sorting the N intervals, with the subsequent linear merge pass taking O(N). Space Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space (excluding the output array and O(log N) or O(N) space utilized by the sorting algorithm implementation).
pseudoCode:
FUNCTION merge(intervals):
    SORT(intervals BY start_time), merged = []
    FOR interval IN intervals DO:
        IF merged IS EMPTY OR LAST(merged).end < interval.start THEN APPEND interval TO merged
        ELSE LAST(merged).end = MAX(LAST(merged).end, interval.end)
    END FOR
    RETURN merged
END FUNCTION
